note: Fictional story. Every character, company, newspaper and broadcast in it is invented and none depicts a real person. The city issues it plays with are real.

prologue.t: Eighteen months. They hand you back a wallet, a watch and forty dollars, and they call it a release.
prologue.d: [low, tired voice] Eighteen months. They hand you back a wallet, a watch, and forty dollars... and they call it a release.

prologue.t: My father fed the mill thirty-one years. It paid him back with a letter. Then the pension went. Then the house. Then him.
prologue.d: [flat, bitter] My father fed the mill thirty-one years. It paid him back with a letter. Then the pension went. Then the house. [quieter] Then him.

prologue.t: I missed the funeral by nine days.
prologue.d: [dry, hollow] I missed the funeral by nine days.

prologue.t: So here is the plan. Ride home. Keep my head down. Start over.
prologue.d: [quiet, resolved] So here is the plan. Ride home. Keep my head down. Start over.

epilogue.t: They did not cancel the ballpark. They tabled it. In this town, that counts as a miracle.
Pruitt still owns half of downtown. Sam prints the news in his garage. Olsen talks now. Loudly.
The library is open Sundays. Marge says I still owe for the book.
Everett is not broke, Danny. It was spending on the wrong things.

chapters.title: LAST CALL

intro.t: Look at this. Dead man's kid, drinking a dead man's whiskey, on a dead man's tab.
intro.d: [gruff, amused] Look at this. Dead man's kid, drinking a dead man's whiskey... on a dead man's tab.

intro.t: You said it was on the house.
intro.d: [dry] You said it was on the house.

intro.t: It is. I'm just narrating.
intro.d: [deadpan] It is. I'm just narrating.

intro.t: Go easy, Olsen. He's been out three hours. He still thinks the parking is free.
intro.d: [light, teasing] Go easy, Olsen. He's been out three hours. He still thinks the parking is free.

intro.t: Sam Reyes. Last time I saw you, you were getting punched for the school paper.
intro.d: [warming up, half smiling] Sam Reyes. Last time I saw you, you were getting punched for the school paper.

intro.t: Still am. Pays worse now.
intro.d: [wry] Still am. [short laugh] Pays worse now.

intro.t: Tell him what you told me.
intro.d: [low, serious] Tell him what you told me.

intro.t: The Kessler Hotel. Burned Tuesday. Fire marshal says wiring. That building's been empty two years, and the power's been cut for one.
intro.d: [lowered voice, serious] The Kessler Hotel. Burned Tuesday. Fire marshal says wiring. That building's been empty two years... and the power's been cut for one.

intro.t: So, no wiring.
intro.d: [flat] So... no wiring.

intro.t: So no wiring. The night clerk, Tomás, was sleeping in the lobby because he had nowhere else to go. He didn't get out.
intro.d: [quiet, heavy] So no wiring. The night clerk, Tomás, was sleeping in the lobby because he had nowhere else to go... He didn't get out.

intro.t: Who owned it?
intro.d: [quiet] Who owned it?

intro.t: Who owns everything with plywood on it? Lyle Pruitt. He buys them tired, lets them rot, and collects when they light up.
intro.d: [bitter, scoffing] Who owns everything with plywood on it? Lyle Pruitt. He buys them tired, lets them rot, and collects when they light up.

intro.t: Fourth one in three years. The permits for the replacement were filed before the smoke cleared. I can't print that. I can't prove who struck the match.
intro.d: [frustrated, tight] Fourth one in three years. The permits for the replacement were filed before the smoke cleared. I can't print that. I can't prove who struck the match.

intro.t: And you're telling me this why?
intro.d: [guarded, suspicious] And you're telling me this... why?

intro.t: Because Pruitt is hiring drivers. Quiet ones. With a record, so they stay quiet.
intro.d: [matter-of-fact] Because Pruitt is hiring drivers. Quiet ones. With a record... so they stay quiet.

intro.t: No.
intro.d: [firm, immediate] No.

intro.t: You'd be inside. One week. You see a name, a truck, a gas can, you call me.
intro.d: [urgent, hushed] You'd be inside. One week. You see a name, a truck, a gas can... you call me.

intro.t: I did eighteen months for doing a favor, Sam. I'm all out of favors.
intro.d: [tired, angry underneath] I did eighteen months for doing a favor, Sam. I'm all out of favors.

intro.t: Your father's pension. Who do you think drew up the bankruptcy that ate it? Pruitt didn't close the mill. He just sold the coffin.
intro.d: [low, hard] Your father's pension. Who do you think drew up the bankruptcy that ate it? Pruitt didn't close the mill. He just sold the coffin.

intro.t: Where's his office?
intro.d: [exhales] ...Where's his office?

intro.t: Commerce Building. Top floor. Wear the jacket. It makes you look employable.
intro.d: [relieved, light] Commerce Building. Top floor. Wear the jacket. It makes you look employable.

intro.t: Barely.
intro.d: [deadpan] Barely.

steps.text: Go see Lyle Pruitt on the top floor of the Commerce Building

radio.t: Don't sell it too hard. Men like him can smell wanting.
radio.d: [low, dry] Don't sell it too hard. Men like him can smell wanting.

lines.t: Walt's boy. I knew your father. Never missed a shift, never asked a question. I admire that in a man.
lines.d: [warm, unhurried] Walt's boy. I knew your father. Never missed a shift, never asked a question. I admire that in a man.

lines.t: He asked one. Where the pension went.
lines.d: [level, cold] He asked one. Where the pension went.

lines.t: Markets. Terrible things. Nobody's fault, and everybody's money.
lines.d: [sighs, faintly amused] Markets. Terrible things. Nobody's fault... and everybody's money.

lines.t: I read your file. Eighteen months for a truck that was not yours, and you never said whose it was. Do you know what that is?
lines.d: [conversational, probing] I read your file. Eighteen months for a truck that was not yours, and you never said whose it was. Do you know what that is?

lines.t: Stupid.
A reference. I have a car in the county lot that should not be there. Grey sedan. My man parked it badly, and then he stopped answering his phone.
lines.d: [pleased, soft] A reference. I have a car in the county lot that should not be there. Grey sedan. My man parked it badly... and then he stopped answering his phone.

lines.t: What's in it?
Upholstery. You bring it to my storage on Rucker, and you do not open the trunk. That is the whole job.
lines.d: [smooth, then quietly firm] Upholstery. You bring it to my storage on Rucker, and you do NOT open the trunk. That is the whole job.

lines.t: And if somebody stops me?
lines.d: [testing him] And if somebody stops me?

lines.t: Then you were never here, and I never knew your father. Four hundred. Cash. Welcome home.
lines.d: [cold, pleasant] Then you were never here, and I never knew your father... Four hundred. Cash. [warm again] Welcome home.

steps.text: Take the grey sedan from the county lot by the courthouse

done.t: You're in? Already? Danny. Whatever is in that car, look at it.
done.d: [surprised, hushed] You're in? Already? [serious] Danny. Whatever is in that car... look at it.

done.t: He said don't open the trunk.
done.d: [muttering] He said don't open the trunk.

done.t: That's how you know which part to open.
done.d: [dry] That's how you know which part to open.

steps.text: County deputies made the plate. Lose them

radio.t: Danny, it's Dee. The scanner just lit up with a grey sedan and your description. Tell me that's a coincidence.
radio.d: [brisk, worried] Danny, it's Dee. The scanner just lit up with a grey sedan and your description. Tell me that's a coincidence.

radio.t: You are a terrible liar. Lose them, and call me.
radio.d: [exasperated] You are a TERRIBLE liar. Lose them, and call me.

steps.text: Bring the sedan to Pruitt's storage on Rucker

outro.t: Don't open the trunk.
outro.d: [under his breath] Don't open the trunk.

outro.t: Two gas cans. Road flares. And a hotel register. The Kessler. Last entry, Tuesday night. Tomás Ibarra. Lobby.
outro.d: [slow, sinking realization] Two gas cans. Road flares. And a hotel register. The Kessler. Last entry... Tuesday night. [quiet] Tomás Ibarra. Lobby.

outro.t: You opened it.
You said upholstery.
I said don't. I needed to know which kind of man you are. A man who looks can be taught not to talk. A man who doesn't look is just a mule.
outro.d: [patient, almost fatherly] I said don't. I needed to know which kind of man you are. A man who looks can be taught not to talk. A man who doesn't look... is just a mule.

outro.t: A man died in that building.
outro.d: [low, shaking with anger] A man died in that building.

outro.t: A man was trespassing in my building. There is a difference, and I own the people who decide it. Go home, Danny. You start Monday.
outro.d: [cold, precise] A man was trespassing in my building. There is a difference, and I own the people who decide it. [lighter] Go home, Danny. You start Monday.

outro.t: Tell me you got something.
outro.d: [eager, hushed] Tell me you got something.

outro.t: I got a job.

chapters.news: Port Gardner Radio news. The fire marshal has closed the Kessler Hotel investigation, citing faulty wiring. A memorial for Tomás Ibarra will be held Friday.

pre.d: [shouting over heavy rain] Hey! HEY! Kill the engine!

pre.t: You did when you were this tall. Olsen. I worked the dock with your old man.
pre.d: [gruff, warm] You did when you were this tall. Olsen. I worked the dock with your old man.

pre.t: And I'm the reason you got detention in tenth grade. Sam Reyes. Welcome out.
pre.d: [quick, friendly] And I'm the reason you got detention in tenth grade. Sam Reyes. [warmly] Welcome out.

pre.t: Home's been sold, kid. Come on. One drink. We need to talk.
pre.d: [quiet, heavy] Home's been sold, kid... [softer] Come on. One drink. We need to talk.

chapters.title: OVERDUE

intro.t: Danny Voss. You still owe us for a book on engine repair. Nineteen ninety eight.
I fixed the engine.
They cut our hours again. Closed Sundays, closed Mondays. The same week they found millions for a ballpark.
What do you want me to do about it, Marge?
I have been back two days. I drive packages for Dee.
Your father read every Zane Grey we had. Twice. He would not let them lock that door without a fight.
Four thousand signatures. The clerk locks the door at five. You drive like your father. So drive.

steps.text: Get the petitions to City Hall before the clerk leaves

radio.t: Danny, it's Dee. City Hall, Wetmore side. And slow down, I can hear your tires from dispatch.
Good to hear your voice too, Dee.

outro.t: Did they take them?
Stamped and filed.
Good. Now they have to pretend to read them.

post.t: Four thousand signatures. About a library.
Mayor, nobody ever cut a ribbon on a library being open on a Sunday.
I want that ballpark open by spring, Lyle.

chapters.news: Port Gardner Radio news. Library hours are cut again as the city faces a budget gap. Officials say the downtown ballpark is still on schedule.

chapters.title: DEMOLITION BY NEGLECT

intro.t: See that cornice? Nineteen twenty five. Lyle Pruitt bought the block, pulled the tenants, and left the windows open all winter.
Why would a man wreck his own building?
Because a ruin is cheaper to tear down than a landmark. They call it demolition by neglect. We call it Tuesday.
Three notices. Culmback, Commerce, McCabe. Once it is posted, it is on the record.

steps.text: Post a notice on the Culmback Building (1/3)

radio.t: A staple gun and a ladder. This is what I came home for.

steps.text: Post a notice on the Commerce Building (2/3)
Post a notice on the McCabe Building (3/3)

lines.t: Son, you are stapling paper to my property.
It's a public notice.
Everything is public until somebody buys it. Lyle Pruitt. I am the reason this town is going to have a skyline.
It had one.
Tell Marge I said hello. And tell her winter is coming.

outro.t: He came down and talked to you himself?
White hat. Big smile.
Then we are finally doing something right.
Marge. Why do you care this much about old brick?
Because I taught half this town to read in rooms like those. You tear down the room, people forget they were ever in it.

chapters.news: Preservation notices appeared overnight on three downtown buildings owned by developer Lyle Pruitt. Pruitt called it vandalism with paperwork.

chapters.title: BALLPARK FIGURE

intro.t: Sam Reyes, Everett Ledger. I am the newsroom. All of it.
Marge said you needed a driver.
What happened to the rest of it?
Bought, sold, and laid off. I kept the keys because nobody asked for them back.
I need a number. The ballpark had a price. Then it had a bigger one. Nobody will show me the estimate.
The contractor keeps the binders in a box truck by the station. I am a reporter. I can't steal a truck.
But you can ask me to.
I would call it sourcing.

steps.text: Take the contractor's box truck near Everett Station

done.t: Danny. That is not your truck.

steps.text: Bring the truck to the Ledger office at the Evergreen Building

outro.t: Look at this. A new total every month, and every one of them stamped final.
Where is the extra going?
That is the story. Somebody is selling the city the dirt under home plate. Guess who owns the dirt.

chapters.news: The Everett Ledger reports the ballpark estimate has grown by tens of millions. Mayor Dale Hargrove calls the number, quote, a rough ballpark figure.

post.t: Somebody took a truck, Lyle. With your binders in it.
Binders are paper, Mayor. Paper burns, paper gets lost, paper gets explained.
You ran on a ballpark. I am just the man who knows what it costs.

chapters.title: RIBBON CUTTING

intro.t: You're the driver? Wonderful. Whit Brannigan, your congressman. I am late for three ribbons.
Three.
A bus shelter, a crane, and a hot dog stand at the arena. Federal dollars at work.
I have a truck full of borrowed binders on my mind, sir.
I did not hear that. I never hear anything. It is how I have lasted.

steps.text: Drive the congressman to Everett Station (1/3)

radio.t: Faster. No, slower, there is a camera. Wave!
Between us. Lyle Pruitt asked my office for federal money for that ballpark. I said, send the paperwork. He never did.
Men with clean deals love paperwork.

steps.text: Last ribbon: Angel of the Winds Arena (3/3)

radio.t: You know what I admire about ribbons? They cannot be audited.
I'm starting to see why you last.

outro.t: You never drove me. But if you had, you were excellent.
Yes sir.
And son? Whatever is in those binders. Read the last page first.

chapters.news: Congressman Whit Brannigan cut three ribbons in under six minutes today. His office is calling it a district record.

chapters.title: EYES ON BROADWAY

intro.t: They fired me this morning. Pruitt bought the Ledger's building. New landlord, new priorities.
So it's over.
I still have a login. The city hung plate cameras on every road into town. Somebody ran a search on Marge's car. And on yours.
Who?
The audit log says who. It is at the service center, on paper, because nobody trusts the system that watches everybody.

steps.text: Pick up the audit at the City Service Center

done.t: Danny, every camera on Broadway just lit up with your plate. They are coming.

steps.text: The cameras saw you. Lose the police

done.t: You're clear. I don't know how. Do not tell me how.

steps.text: Bring the audit back to Sam at the courthouse

outro.t: The searches came from a contractor account. Pruitt Development. He is using the city's cameras like a doorbell.
Can you print it?
I don't have a paper anymore. I have a printer.
Danny Voss. Every man in this town has a number. I am calling to ask yours.
My dad's was thirty one years. You could not afford him either.

chapters.news: Questions tonight about who can see the city's license plate camera logs. The police chief says the system is working as intended.

chapters.title: STRUCTURAL DEFICIT

intro.t: Your old man loaded pulp on this dock. He would hate what I am about to tell you.
Pruitt has been paying me to move cars out through the old mill site. Tonight it is a gold coupe with a trunk that sits low.
Cash.
The kind that never saw a bank. The kind that buys a vote before a meeting.
Why tell me?
They closed the mill and I said nothing. I am done saying nothing.

steps.text: Take Pruitt's gold coupe at the old mill site

done.t: That is my car, son. Bring it back and I will forget your face.
You already ran my plate. You know exactly who I am.

steps.text: Get the coupe to Marge at the library in one piece

outro.t: Good lord. How much is in there?
Enough to keep the lights on Sundays for about a hundred years.
I shelved books in this building for forty years. Nobody ever brought me a trunk.
We cannot keep it, Danny.
No. But we can bring it to the meeting and ask the mayor whose it is.

chapters.news: Developer Lyle Pruitt reports a gold coupe stolen from the old mill site. He declined to say what was in the trunk.

chapters.title: PUBLIC COMMENT

intro.t: The council votes at seven. Three minutes at the microphone. That is all a citizen gets.
I have the binders, the audit, and a trunk of cash with his name on the bands.
Then you do the talking.
No. They have heard me for forty years. They have never heard you.

steps.text: Get to City Hall before the vote. Every cop in town is looking for you

radio.t: The whole department is looking for you, Danny. You picked a real quiet night.

lines.t: You are the driver. I was born here too, son. Colby Avenue. I wanted to build one thing before I am done.
Then build the thing we asked you for.
It is not that simple.
It never is, until somebody says it out loud. I am about to say it out loud.
Public comment is closed.
It's six fifty eight. Danny Voss. Born on Rucker, raised on Rockefeller.
My dad worked the mill. When it closed, you told us there was no money. No money for the library. No money for the old buildings. No money for anything that was already ours.
Here is the estimate you never showed us. Here is who has been running our plates. And here is a trunk of cash from the man who sells you the dirt.
This is theater.
No sir. Theater is the ribbon cuttings. This is public comment.
The chair moves to table the vote.

outro.t: Three minutes. You used two.
I ran out of things to say.
No you didn't. You just said them once.

chapters.news: A surprise at City Hall tonight. The council tabled the ballpark vote after public comment ran four hours. Mayor Hargrove says he looks forward to further study.
